newsitem.title: USA: Cunanan's death opens up new murder probes.
newsitem.headline: Cunanan's death opens up new murder probes.

text.p: Police Tuesday asked for fingerprint and DNA samples from Andrew Cunanan's body to determine if the man accused of murdering fashion designer Gianni Versace also was behind the unsolved murders of three gay men.

San Diego homicide Lt. Jim Collins told Reuters, "This is the first time anyone has been able to get their hands on Cunanan's DNA and fingerprints. We are going to be comparing those samples with evidence left at the scenes of these three murders."
But he stressed that investigators were looking as much to eliminate Cunanan from the murders as to linking him to them.
If nothing else, Cunanan's DNA typing and prints will help confirm suspicions held by police from California to Florida who have attributed five murders to the gay hustler-turned-spree killer.
Collins said he did not know if police probing other unsolved murders elsewhere in the country might also want to use the newly acquired scientific evidence.

Cunanan's ashes were to have been flown to San Diego from Miami this week, but authorities refused to say if they arrived and Cunanan's family has gone into seclusion and asked the press to respect their privacy.

Cunanan, 27, shot himself to death on July 15 in Miami Beach, two miles (three km) from the scene where Versace was gunned down outside his mansion eight days earlier. Police believe Versace was the fifth victim of Cunanan's cross-country killing spree.
Of the three unsolved San Diego murders previously not connected with Cunanan, the first was that of Todd Loren, a 32-year-old gay man who was a successful comic book publisher.
Loren was bludgeoned and stabbed to death in his apartment in San Diego's Hillcrest district, centre of the city's gay community, in 1992.
Loren's parents, Herb and Marilyn Shapiro, recently called the San Diego police saying their son may have been romantically involved with Cunanan and might have been killed by him.

Collins cautioned that police have a suspect in that case -- a man found driving Loren's stolen car in San Francisco -- but did not have enough evidence to charge him. But he added "We have one piece of evidence that we can't attribute to the victim or the suspect, and we'll be comparing that to Cunanan's DNA." He declined to say what the evidence was.
"We have absolutely nothing to link Cunanan to him (Loren) but we are going to go ahead and do some samples," he said.
Collins declined to name the other two victims or describe their cases, except to say that both were gay men who were killed in or near the Hillcrest area over the past two years.

"We've got some evidence (from the unsolved murders), fingerprints and blood evidence that we'll be using to compare with (Cunanan's) DNA and fingerprints. Beyond that I'm not saying just what the evidence is," Collins said.
He added that he did not know when San Diego police would receive Cunanan's fingerprints and DNA printout, but said it would be several weeks before investigators had any results.

Cunanan, who police say moved in the gay community's high circles and lived off "benefactors" and wealthy, older friends, remains the only suspect in the killings of Jeffrey Trail, a former naval office; David Madson, an ex-lover; Chicago real estate developer Lee Miglin, and William Reese, a cemetery caretaker.
